name: Diastema closure

lead: A diastema is a space between two teeth, most often between the upper front teeth. Diastema closure is any dental treatment that closes that space so the front teeth meet evenly, for a smile many people see as more regular.

The options include tooth-coloured composite bonding, porcelain veneers, braces or other orthodontic appliances, and sometimes a minor gum-tissue procedure when a low-attached frenulum is involved. Clinical studies, mostly small, report that composite closures survive for years with occasional repairs.

paras: A dentist assesses the cause of the gap first. Bonding builds up the sides of the teeth in resin in a single visit and is reversible in principle. Veneers use thin porcelain shells. Orthodontic closure moves the teeth together using braces, aligners, springs or retainers, sometimes after a frenectomy.

Restorations can chip, stain or need replacement; bonded resin may wear faster than porcelain. Closing a gap that is caused by tooth-size mismatch can leave teeth looking wide unless reshaping is planned. Orthodontic closure can relapse without retention. A gap itself is not a disease, and the decision is cosmetic.

angle.text: Bonding, veneers or braces bring the front teeth together so there is no visible gap. People who prefer an even smile use it to change how their front teeth look.

lead: Diastema closure is the cosmetic or orthodontic treatment of a space between teeth, most often between the upper central incisors. A diastema usually results from teeth being small relative to the jaw, and other causes include a large or low-set labial frenulum, gum disease, an extra tooth (mesiodens), or forward-tilted front teeth.[1]

For appearance, closure aims at a more continuous, symmetrical front-tooth line. The main approaches are direct composite resin bonding, porcelain veneers, and orthodontic tooth movement, with a frenectomy sometimes included when tissue is part of the cause.[1][2][3]

Reception of gaps varies by culture: in parts of West and East Africa a gap is often considered attractive, and in France it is traditionally called "dents du bonheur" (lucky teeth). Closing it is therefore a personal preference.[1]

paras: A diastema is common in children and can persist into adulthood. It is not in itself a disease, and treatment is largely cosmetic. Causes include tooth-to-jaw size mismatch, a prominent frenulum, periodontal bone loss, a mesiodens, skeletal mismatch and proclined incisors, and the treatment is chosen to suit the cause.[1]

Resin composite is added to the sides of the teeth to close the gap. Technique papers describe matrix and contact-forming methods, and a trial on artificial teeth compared Teflon tape, pull-through and Bioclear matrix techniques for forming contacts and avoiding voids.[4] Older dental literature describes composite closure as a long-established approach.[5][6]
Sectional feldspathic porcelain veneers placed under a dental microscope have been used to close midline gaps with minimal tooth preparation.[7]
Appliances such as an M-spring after a frenectomy, vacuum-formed retainers, and magnets have been reported for moving teeth together.[8][9][10]

A randomized trial of 23 patients compared two nanohybrid composite resins for diastema closure and tooth reshaping over four years; 58 restorations in 19 patients were evaluated at a mean of 43.4 months, with a few repaired for partial fracture and survival rates reported at 96.3% for one material.[3]

A case series of five patients with stable midline diastema followed sectional porcelain veneers for up to four years using World Dental Federation criteria.[7] A 2024 case report described complete closure within four months with an M-spring after frenectomy.[8]
Dental appearance is a common topic in looksmaxxing discussions, where a gap closure is one of several smile changes people discuss, together with whitening, aligners and veneers.
